subject: Time series forecasting: describing a series over time, and forecasting it with benchmark, exponential smoothing and ARIMA methods, evaluated honestly
outOfScope: State space models for exponential smoothing (ETS likelihoods and the error, trend, seasonal taxonomy in depth), and Kalman filtering
Deep learning and machine learning forecasters, such as LSTMs, transformers and gradient-boosted trees
Multivariate models such as vector autoregression (VAR), and dynamic regression with ARIMA errors
Causal impact analysis and intervention analysis
Hierarchical and grouped forecasting, and forecast reconciliation
Judgmental forecasting, for when there is no data
Volatility models such as ARCH and GARCH
Box-Cox transformation details, bias adjustment and back-transformation
Multiple seasonality and sub-daily data, and irregularly spaced series
The mathematics of estimation (maximum likelihood) and of unit root test statistics
Software specifics, such as R's fable package or Python's statsmodels

concepts.title: What a time series is, and what forecasting it means
concepts.outcome: Say what makes data a time series, what forecasting one aims to do, and what a model of a series can be used for.

keyPoints.text: Anything observed one after another over time is a time series; the book works with series recorded at regular intervals. Forecasting one means estimating how the sequence of observations will continue into the future.

keyPoints.text: The simplest time series methods use only the past of the variable being forecast. They carry its trend and seasonal patterns forward but ignore everything else, such as marketing, competitors or changes in the economy.

keyPoints.text: A cycle is a rise and fall that does not have a fixed frequency. Cycles are often due to economic conditions, such as the business cycle, and usually last at least two years.

concepts.title: Autocorrelation and the ACF
concepts.outcome: Read an ACF plot and recognise the signatures of trend and seasonality in it.

keyPoints.text: Autocorrelation measures the linear relationship between lagged values of a series: the lag-1 coefficient relates each value to the one before it, the lag-2 coefficient to the one two periods before, and so on.

keyPoints.text: The autocorrelation coefficients together make up the autocorrelation function, or ACF. It is usually plotted against the lag, and the plot is sometimes called a correlogram.

keyPoints.text: With a trend, autocorrelations at small lags are large and positive, because observations close in time are close in value, so the ACF of a trended series declines slowly as the lag grows.

concepts.title: Stationarity
concepts.outcome: Decide whether a series is stationary from its time plot, and say why many methods need it.

keyPoints.text: A stationary series has statistical properties that do not depend on when it is observed. Series with trend or seasonality are therefore not stationary, while white noise is: it looks much the same whenever you observe it.

keyPoints.text: A stationary series has no predictable long-term patterns. Its time plot looks roughly horizontal, with constant variance, though some cyclic behaviour is possible.

keyPoints.text: Many time series techniques assume stationarity, meaning the mean, variance and autocorrelation structure do not change over time: in practice, a flat-looking series without trend, changing variance or seasonality.

Patterns are described in a series observed over time.
A decomposition separates the trend-cycle and seasonal patterns.
Seasonal adjustment removes a component found by decomposition.
Classical decomposition and STL are ways of computing a decomposition.
The ACF is read for the signatures of trend and seasonality.
White noise is defined by having no autocorrelation.
White noise is the simplest stationary series.
Stationarity rules out trend and seasonality.
Spurious regression comes from regressing non-stationary series.
Differencing is a way to make a series stationary.
The ACF is used to judge whether differencing is needed.
Seasonal differencing extends first differencing to the seasonal lag.
Choosing among the benchmarks depends on whether the data are trended or seasonal.
The random walk explains why the naive and drift methods work.
A random walk is a series whose differences are white noise.
Residual checks are first applied to the benchmark methods.
Good residuals look like white noise.
Prediction intervals rest on assumptions about the residuals.
Test-set evaluation is needed because residuals understate forecast error.
Accuracy measures summarise errors on a test set.
Cross-validation averages an accuracy measure over many test sets.

Holt's method adds a trend to simple exponential smoothing.
